pdm-ventricular-heart-blocks: Where does ventricular tachycardia originate?
In the ventricles: any tachycardia arising there
What rate range defines ventricular tachycardia?
100 to 300 per minute
What is the QRS width in ventricular tachycardia?
Wide
What do P waves look like in ventricular tachycardia?
Absent, or dissociated from the QRS complexes
Can ventricular tachycardia have a pulse?
Yes: it presents with or without a pulse
What separates monomorphic from polymorphic ventricular tachycardia?
Monomorphic is regular with one shape; polymorphic is irregular and changes shape
What is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia commonly called?
Torsades de pointes
What does torsades de pointes mean?
Twisting of the points
What is torsades de pointes usually a consequence of?
A prolonged QT interval
What is the regularity of torsades de pointes?
Irregular
What mechanism produces ventricular fibrillation?
Chaotic firing of multiple foci within the ventricles
What rate range is listed for ventricular fibrillation?
300 to 500 per minute
Which waves are measurable in ventricular fibrillation?
None: no P waves, QRS complexes or T waves
Why is there no pulse in ventricular fibrillation?
The ventricles quiver and do not contract
What is the cardiac output in ventricular fibrillation?
None
What separates ventricular tachycardia from ventricular fibrillation?
Tachycardia is organized; fibrillation is chaotic with no measurable QRS
What is fine ventricular fibrillation?
Low-amplitude chaotic waves that can resemble a flat line
What is asystole?
No electrical activity and no pulse: a flat line
What does untreated ventricular fibrillation end in?
Asystole
What is pulseless electrical activity?
Organized electrical activity with no mechanical activity
What can pulseless electrical activity look like on the monitor?
Any organized rhythm, even normal sinus
What makes an organized rhythm pulseless electrical activity?
The absence of a pulse
What does ventricular standstill show on the strip?
Upright P waves marching across with no QRS complexes
What is the cardiac output in ventricular standstill?
None: the atria contract but the ventricles do not
What separates ventricular standstill from asystole?
Standstill keeps its P waves; asystole has none
What does an atrial paced beat look like?
A pacer spike followed by a normal P-QRS-T cycle
What does an atrial pacemaker depend on?
An intact, properly functioning conduction pathway
Which three findings show ventricular capture?
A spike before every QRS, a wide QRS and a contralateral T wave
What is a contralateral T wave?
A T wave pointing opposite to its QRS complex
Why is a ventricular paced QRS wide?
The ventricles are paced below the level of the atria
What is an atrioventricular heart block?
Delayed or failed conduction of an atrial impulse through the atrioventricular node
What are the two other names for second-degree type I block?
Wenckebach and Mobitz I
What is another name for second-degree type II block?
Mobitz II
What is another name for third-degree block?
Complete heart block
What is the hallmark of first-degree block?
A sinus rhythm with a PR interval beyond 0.2 seconds
Which P waves are conducted in first-degree block?
All of them
How is first-degree block characterized?
Benign
Where is the delay in first-degree block?
Slowed conduction through the atrioventricular node
Which measurement diagnoses first-degree block?
The PR interval duration
What does the PR do in second-degree type I?
Lengthens beat to beat until a P wave is not conducted
What is the classic pattern of second-degree type I?
Grouped beats ending in a dropped QRS, then the cycle restarts
What happens to atrioventricular nodal conduction in Wenckebach block?
It slows beat by beat until one impulse is not conducted
Where is the block in second-degree type I?
In the atrioventricular node
What does the PR do in second-degree type II?
Stays constant across the strip
How does type II compare with type I?
Less common but more serious
What does second-degree type II always indicate?
Underlying disease of the conduction system
Where is the block in second-degree type II?
Below the atrioventricular node, in the His-Purkinje system
How many conducted beats with a constant PR identify type II?
At least two consecutive ones before the dropped QRS
Can type II drop more than one beat in a row?
Yes
What is the QRS usually like in type II?
Usually wide, from an accompanying bundle branch block, but can be narrow
How do you tell type I from type II at a dropped beat?
Compare the PR before and after it: different is type I, equal is type II
What is the hallmark of third-degree block?
Regular P-P intervals unrelated to regular R-R intervals
How do P waves behave in third-degree block?
They march through the QRS-T complexes
How many P waves are conducted in third-degree block?
None
Which rate is faster in third-degree block?
The atrial rate
Which two pacemakers drive the heart in complete block?
The sinoatrial node and a junctional or ventricular escape
What decides QRS width in third-degree block?
Where the escape rhythm originates
Where does a narrow escape come from in complete block?
The atrioventricular junction
What are the most common causes of third-degree block?
Age-related fibrosis and acute myocardial infarction
Which infarct location is especially linked to complete block?
Inferior
